idiom_name: throw / rejected promise at the first violated precondition; uncaught exceptions terminate by default
implementation_notes: throw is syntax in JavaScript: it stops the current function, skips the rest of it, and unwinds to the first catch - and if none exists, Node prints the stack trace and exits with code 1, which is the fail-fast baseline the runtime already implements. Async code fails fast through a rejected Promise; the flag --abort-on-uncaught-exception upgrades that default exit to a V8 abort (core dump) when an unhandled exception should not be resumable. What replaces the classic structure is therefore nothing new: the discipline is refusing to subvert the language's own termination path with empty catches, .catch(() => {}) handlers and error-first callbacks that never check the first argument.
pitfalls: An empty catch, a .catch(() => {}) (or resolving instead of rejecting) silently converts the fail-fast path; the --unhandled-rejections policy decides whether a missed rejection crashes or is only warned about.
A throw inside an async callback or a Promise executor escapes the surrounding try block, so guards must sit inside the async boundary they are meant to protect.
TypeError only fires on property access of null/undefined: shape and range validation needs explicit checks (or a schema validator), otherwise invalid data flows on to fail much later.
